Sensitivity analyses looking at misspecification of the effect of statins and antihypertensives

26 August 2026

  • 1 Sensitivity analysis in entire validation cohort
    • 1.1 Women
    • 1.2 Men
  • 2 Treatment-stratified sensitivity analysis
    • 2.1 Women; Statins; not on treatment at baseline
    • 2.2 Women; Statins; on treatment at baseline
    • 2.3 Women; antihypertensives; not on treatment at baseline
    • 2.4 Women; antihypertensives; on treatment at baseline
    • 2.5 Men; Statins; not on treatment at baseline
    • 2.6 Men; Statins; on treatment at baseline
    • 2.7 Men; antihypertensives; not on treatment at baseline
    • 2.8 Men; antihypertensives; on treatment at baseline

Associated manuscript: A flexible approach to sequential prediction under intervention

These supplementary analyses validate the model under the assumption that the treatment effect of statins and antihypertensives in the validation dataset are 10% and 20% bigger/smaller than those assumed in the development dataset when building the model. We refer to this as a misspecification of the treatment effect (i.e., the treatment effect in the development dataset has been misspecified compared to the true effect in the validation dataset).

We multiply the effect of statins or antihypertensives (on the hazard ratio scale) by values of 0.8, 0.9, 1.1 and 1.2. Given that the hazard ratios for statin and antihypertensive use are < 1, the multipliers 0.8 and 0.9 correspond to a bigger effect in the validation dataset, and multipliers 1.1 and 1.2 correspond to a smaller effect in the validation dataset.

In order to assess the impact of misspecification, we estimate counterfactual survival times in the validation dataset (see supplementary material for this process) using these miss-specified treatment effects. After this, calibration and discrimination are assessed in the way as described in the main manuscript, and supplementary file 1 (methodology).

In section 1, we report calibration and discrimination in the entire validation dataset, for various levels of misspecification of the treatment effect of statins/antihypertensives. For calibration, we report calibration curves, and the confidence interval for the calibration curve (note, the confidence intervals in section 1 are very small and so are not visible), and summary metrics ICI, E50 and E90. For discrimination, Harrell's C-index is reported. In section 2, we repeat the analyses within subgroups defined by treatment use (either statins or antihypertensives) at baseline. This is because we expect the biggest effect to be among individuals who are on treatment at baseline. The cohort of individuals off treatment at baseline contains a large number of individuals who never receive any treatment, and are therefore unaffected by the misspecification.

Calibration and discrimination are always compared with an analysis assuming there is no misspecification of the treatment effects, aligned with the primary analysis from the main manuscript.

1 Sensitivity analysis in entire validation cohort

In the following tables and plots (section 1), 'no misspecification' is the same value from the primary analysis, assuming no misspecification of the treatment effect. 'Difference' is the difference between the sensitivity analysis value, and the 'no misspecification' value.

When the treatment effects are miss-specified by 10%/20% we see negligible changes to model performance. This will be for two reasons. Firstly, the calibration and discrimination metrics are dominated by low risk individuals who have a small probability of receiving treatment, among whom the impact of misspecification of the treatment is small. Although, it should be noted that misspecification seems to have minimal effect among high risk individuals too. This could be partially due to the second reason, which is that the cohort is a mix of individuals on and off treatment at baseline. If equal numbers of individuals start/stop taking treatment during follow-up, the effect of the misspecification would cancel out. This is why we look at stratified analyses within those on/off treatment at baseline (see section 2).

2 Treatment-stratified sensitivity analysis

In the following tables and plots (section 2), 'no misspecification' is an estimate assuming no misspecification of the treatment effect (i.e. aligned with the primary analysis), but stratified to the same subgroup. 'Difference' is the difference between the sensitivity analysis value, and the 'no misspecification' value.

As expected, misspecification of the effects of either statins/antihypertensives has a bigger impact on calibration and discrimination among those on the respective treatment at baseline.

For example, consider section 2.2.1, or 2.6.1. When the effect of statins is bigger in the validation cohort (statins multiplier = 0.8 or 0.9), the calibration curve indicates more over-prediction than the calibration curve under no misspecification. Similarly, when the effect of statins is smaller in the validation cohort (statins multiplier = 1.1 or 1.2), the calibration curve indicates less over-prediction. Despite this, the magnitude of the difference in the calibration curves is not alarming, and is only visible among higher risk individuals.

Note, the calibration within subgroups defined by treatment use at baseline is imperfect, even when there is no misspecification of the treatment effect between development and validation. This will largely be due to the fact that statin and antihypertensive use is a strong predictor of incident cardiovascular disease, which have not been used as predictors in the model. This effect is much stronger for the statin users group (sections 2.2 and 2.6) compared to the antihypertensive users group (sections 2.4 and 2.8), where the model is reasonably well calibrated across the entire distribution of predicted risk. This trade off between predictive performance in the classical sense, and the ability to use the model for prediction under these interventions, is discussed in the main manuscript.
